title: HPV Vaccination: Who, When, and How Many Doses
body:
What it is

Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination is a preventive vaccine given before exposure to the HPV types it covers. In plain words, it teaches the immune system to recognise certain HPV types so that a later exposure is less likely to lead to infection by those types. It is routinely offered in childhood and early adolescence, and it is a prevention step, not a treatment for an infection that is already present.

How it works

Vaccination is usually given as an injection in the upper arm. Guidance commonly used in many programmes is routine vaccination at ages 11 to 12, with vaccination able to start at age 9, and a two-dose series when the series starts before age 15, compared with a three-dose series when it starts at age 15 or later or for people with weakened immunity. Exact ages, doses, and intervals follow current local guidance, so the schedule should always be confirmed with a clinician or local health service.

What to expect

Expect a brief clinic visit for each dose, a sore arm for a day or two, and sometimes tiredness or a mild headache. Serious reactions are uncommon, and clinic staff observe people briefly after vaccination. Keeping the vaccination record matters, because later care, including screening, still depends on knowing what was given and when.

Limits

Vaccination covers only the HPV types included in the vaccine, so it does not prevent infection by every HPV type, and it does not remove the need for screening. The vaccine prevents infection by covered types; it does not treat an infection that is already present. Protection is strongest when the series is completed before exposure to the covered types. People who start later still benefit from completing the series as advised by a clinician.

Aftercare and follow-up

After each dose, note the date, keep the record somewhere safe, and book the next dose before leaving if one is due. If a dose is missed, ask a clinician how to complete the series rather than restarting on your own. Any worrying reaction after vaccination should be reported to a clinician promptly.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Vaccination Catch-Up: Starting or Finishing Later
body:
What it is

Catch-up vaccination means starting or finishing the HPV vaccine series later than the routine childhood ages. It exists because many people missed the routine offer, moved, changed clinics, or simply did not know about it at the time. Catch-up does not mean it is too late: a clinician can advise whether vaccination is still recommended and how many doses are needed.

How it works

Catch-up starts with checking records: previous doses, ages at each dose, and any clinic notes. A clinician then advises the number of remaining doses and the spacing between them, which depends on the age at the first dose and on immune status. The doses themselves are given the same way as routine doses, in a clinic setting.

What to expect

Expect the same brief visit and sore arm as routine vaccination, and expect the clinician to ask about previous doses and health history first. If records are incomplete, the clinician may advise based on what can be verified and on current guidance rather than guessing.

Limits

Catch-up vaccination does not treat an existing infection or an existing wart, and it does not replace screening. Its value is prevention against covered types not yet encountered, so it is one part of prevention rather than a complete solution on its own.

Aftercare and follow-up

After a catch-up dose, update the vaccination record, book any remaining dose, and keep the record with screening records. If you are unsure whether a dose was given, bring every record you can find to the visit and let the clinician reconcile them.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Screening With Pap and HPV Tests: What Happens and How Often
body:
What it is

Screening means checking for early changes caused by HPV before they cause symptoms. The two main tests are the Pap test, which looks at cells from the cervix for abnormal changes, and the HPV test, which checks for high-risk HPV types. Screening does not prevent infection, but it finds changes early, when follow-up and treatment are simplest.

How it works

A screening visit usually involves a speculum examination so a small sample of cervical cells can be collected, which takes a few minutes and may feel uncomfortable but is usually brief. The sample is sent to a laboratory, and results arrive later. The clinician explains what the result means and whether routine screening, a repeat test, or a closer look is next.

What to expect

Expect brief discomfort during collection and a wait for results. Most results are normal or show changes that need only routine follow-up. An abnormal result does not mean cancer: it usually means closer monitoring or a further examination is needed, and the clinician explains the next step.

Limits

Screening has limits: no test catches every change, results can occasionally be unclear, and screening only helps when follow-up happens. Screening is for people with a cervix, and the right programme depends on age and history, so personal advice comes from a clinician.

Aftercare and follow-up

After screening, note the result date and the next due date, and keep the appointment for any follow-up examination. If a result is unclear or a follow-up is recommended, do not wait for symptoms: attend the follow-up and ask the clinician to explain the result in plain language.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Screening After Vaccination: Why It Is Still Needed
body:
What it is

Vaccination does not end the need for screening. This surprises many people, because it feels as if vaccination should settle the matter. It does not, for two plain reasons: the vaccine covers only some HPV types, and a person may already have encountered a type before vaccination. Screening therefore continues on the usual schedule after vaccination.

How it works

Screening after vaccination works exactly as it does without vaccination: the same sample collection, the same laboratory tests, and the same follow-up pathway if a result needs a closer look. The only difference is the person's history, which the clinician notes so results are read in context.

What to expect

Expect the same brief visit and the same wait for results. Some people feel frustrated at being called for screening after vaccination; that feeling is common, and the reason is protection against the types and exposures vaccination cannot cover.

Limits

The limit here is a misunderstanding, not a medical gap: vaccination plus screening together give stronger protection than either alone, while vaccination alone leaves the uncovered types and any earlier exposure unmonitored. Skipping screening after vaccination removes that second layer of protection.

Aftercare and follow-up

After vaccination, keep the screening due date on the calendar and attend it as usual. If a screening invitation arrives after vaccination, treat it as expected, not as a mistake, and ask the clinician if you are unsure why it was sent.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Safer Sex: Reducing HPV Transmission Risk
body:
What it is

Safer sex means steps that lower, but do not eliminate, the chance of passing HPV between partners. HPV spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, including contact that condoms do not fully cover, which is why safer sex reduces risk without removing it. The steps are practical and ordinary: barrier protection, fewer exposures, and honest conversation with partners.

How it works

In practice, safer sex means using a new condom correctly for each act of intercourse, considering barrier protection for other forms of contact as a clinician advises, and keeping supplies available so protection is not skipped for convenience. It also means pausing and seeking advice if warts or symptoms appear, rather than continuing as normal.

What to expect

Expect safer sex to require planning and conversation rather than a single purchase. Condoms can break or slip, and that happens occasionally; if it does, the sensible step is to note it, consider what follow-up a clinician advises, and continue with protection afterwards.

Limits

The main limit is coverage: condoms do not cover all skin that can carry HPV, and HPV can be present without visible warts or symptoms. Safer sex therefore lowers risk but cannot be presented as full protection, and it never replaces vaccination or screening.

Aftercare and follow-up

After any concern, such as a broken barrier or a new symptom, seek clinician advice promptly and keep to the screening schedule. Routine hygiene, such as washing after contact, is general cleanliness and is not a method of removing or treating HPV.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Smoking Cessation: Why Quitting Helps Against Persistent HPV
body:
What it is

Smoking does not cause HPV infection, but it makes persistent infection more likely, and persistent infection is what leads to lasting cell changes. Quitting smoking is therefore a genuine part of HPV prevention, not a general health lecture added for decoration. The benefit is that the body's defences recover, giving it a better chance of clearing an infection rather than letting it persist.

How it works

Quitting usually starts with setting a quit date, removing cigarettes from the home and daily routine, and asking a clinician about support options, which may include counselling and approved nicotine replacement or prescribed aids where appropriate. The choice of aid, if any, is a clinician decision based on the person's history.

What to expect

Expect cravings and irritability in the first weeks, with gradual improvement over time. Slips happen and are common; a slip is a reason to ask for more support, not a reason to abandon the attempt. Tracking smoke-free days helps make progress visible.

Limits

Quitting has limits as an HPV measure: it improves the odds of clearance and lowers the risk associated with persistence, but it does not prevent infection by itself and does not replace vaccination or screening. People who have smoked for many years still benefit from quitting.

Aftercare and follow-up

After quitting, keep screening appointments, note smoke-free milestones, and ask a clinician for extra support if cravings return strongly. If cessation aids are used, follow the clinician's written instructions and report side effects rather than adjusting doses on your own.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: HPV Education: Knowing What HPV Is and Is Not
body:
What it is

HPV education means giving people accurate, plain facts: HPV is a very common virus, most infections clear on their own, some types can cause warts, and a small number of high-risk types can cause cell changes that, over years, can lead to cancer if unmonitored. Knowing these facts reduces fear and stigma and makes vaccination and screening decisions easier.

How it works

Education works best in short, repeated doses: a leaflet or lesson at school, a conversation at a clinic visit, and a reminder when an invitation for vaccination or screening arrives. Good education names the virus, explains transmission in clinical terms, states what vaccination and screening each do, and gives a clear next step.

What to expect

Expect education to raise questions, especially about stigma: HPV is common, it is not a mark of character, and having it does not mean a partner has been unfaithful, since infection can remain undetected for a long time. A clinician can answer personal questions that a leaflet cannot.

Limits

Education has limits: facts alone do not vaccinate or screen anyone, and misinformation spreads faster than corrections. Education must therefore always end with an action, such as booking a vaccine or screening appointment, and a clinician contact.

Aftercare and follow-up

After learning about HPV, turn knowledge into action: check vaccination status, check the next screening due date, and share accurate information rather than rumours. If anything learned causes worry, raise it with a clinician rather than searching for reassurance online alone.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Partner Communication: Talking Honestly About HPV
body:
What it is

Partner communication means telling a partner, in plain and respectful language, about HPV risk, vaccination, screening, and any warts or test results that affect them. It is part of prevention because partners share exposure, and because decisions about protection and follow-up work better when both people know the facts. It is also a matter of respect: a partner cannot make informed choices without information.

How it works

A conversation usually works best in a private, calm setting, starting with the facts: what HPV is, what is known and unknown in this case, what protection steps are planned, and what the clinician has advised. It helps to agree practical steps together, such as barrier use, vaccination checks, and screening appointments.

What to expect

Expect the conversation to be awkward, and expect questions that cannot be answered on the spot. It is fine to say that a question needs a clinician's answer and to come back to it after a visit. A partner may feel worried or upset; listening matters as much as explaining.

Limits

Communication has limits: it cannot guarantee a partner's choices, and it does not replace medical steps. If a conversation feels unsafe, or if there is any risk of harm, the person should seek support from a clinician or a trusted support service first and prioritise personal safety.

Aftercare and follow-up

After the conversation, note any agreed steps and any unanswered questions, and raise the unanswered questions at the next clinician visit. If a partner develops symptoms or receives a result, encourage prompt clinician advice and keep to the screening schedule.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Cryotherapy: Clinician Freezing Treatment for Warts
body:
What it is

Cryotherapy is a clinician treatment that freezes wart tissue using a very cold substance, usually liquid nitrogen, applied in a clinic. The cold damages the wart tissue so that it separates and heals over the following days and weeks. It is one of the most commonly used clinician treatments for external warts, and it is performed by trained staff, not by the patient.

How it works

Treatment happens in a clinic: the clinician examines the area, confirms the diagnosis, protects surrounding skin as needed, and applies the cold substance for a short, controlled time. The visit is brief, and the clinician explains what healing to expect and when to return if the wart remains.

What to expect

Expect stinging or pain during application, followed by redness, swelling, and often a blister over the next day or two. The blister dries and the area heals over one to three weeks. Some people need more than one session, spaced weeks apart, before the wart is gone.

Limits

Cryotherapy has limits: it treats the visible wart, not the underlying infection, and the wart can return in the same place or nearby. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. It may also leave temporary changes in skin colour, and it is not suitable for every location or every person, which the clinician assesses.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare is hygiene and observation only: keep the area clean and dry, leave any blister undisturbed, avoid picking at healing skin, and contact a clinician if there is increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, or the area does not heal. Attend the review appointment even if the area looks healed.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Clinician-Prescribed Topical Treatments for Warts
body:
What it is

Some warts are treated with medicines applied to the skin, prescribed by a clinician after examination. These treatments are not shop-bought wart products used on guesswork: the clinician chooses the preparation, explains how to apply it, and sets the review date. The patient applies the prescribed preparation exactly as instructed and returns for review.

How it works

Treatment starts with a clinician examination and a written set of instructions: which preparation, how much, how often, and for how long, plus what irritation is expected and what should prompt a call. The patient follows those written instructions and keeps the review appointment so the clinician can judge whether the treatment is working.

What to expect

Expect gradual change over weeks rather than overnight disappearance, and expect some redness or soreness where the preparation is applied. If irritation is strong, the usual step is to contact the clinician for advice rather than stopping silently or increasing the amount.

Limits

Topical treatment has limits: it treats the visible wart, and the wart can return after treatment ends. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. It is also unsuitable for some locations, including internal areas, and it must never be used on broken skin or on a different person than the one it was prescribed for.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare is hygiene and adherence only: wash hands after application, keep the area clean, follow the clinician's written instructions exactly, and attend review. If the area becomes very painful, swollen, or infected-looking, contact a clinician promptly rather than continuing unchanged.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Excision Procedures: Surgical Removal by a Clinician
body:
What it is

Excision means a clinician surgically removes a wart in a clinic or minor-procedure setting, using sterile instruments and, usually, local anaesthetic so the area is numb. It is chosen when other treatments have not worked, when the diagnosis needs confirming by laboratory examination, or when a single larger wart is best removed in one procedure.

How it works

The procedure usually involves numbing the area, removing the wart tissue, managing any bleeding, and closing or dressing the wound. The visit takes longer than a freezing session, and the clinician explains wound care, activity limits, and the review or suture-removal date before the patient leaves.

What to expect

Expect numbness during the procedure, soreness afterwards as the anaesthetic wears off, and a wound that needs days to weeks to heal depending on size and location. A scar may remain, and the clinician explains what is normal healing and what should prompt a call.

Limits

Excision has limits: it removes the visible wart and allows laboratory confirmation, but it does not remove the virus from the surrounding skin. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. New warts can appear nearby, and the procedure itself carries small risks of bleeding, infection, and scarring.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare is hygiene and wound observation only: keep the dressing clean and dry as instructed, change dressings only as the clinician directs, avoid strenuous activity affecting the wound until advised, and contact a clinician for increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, bleeding that does not stop, or a wound that opens. Attend suture removal and review as booked.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Electrocautery: Heat-Based Clinician Removal
body:
What it is

Electrocautery is a clinician treatment that uses a controlled electric current to generate heat in a small probe, which removes wart tissue in a clinic setting under local anaesthetic. It is used for warts that have not responded to simpler treatments, or where precise removal of a defined area is wanted. Like every removal method here, it is performed by trained staff, not by the patient.

How it works

The procedure involves numbing the area, applying the probe to the wart tissue for controlled periods, and dressing the resulting small wound. The clinician explains the expected healing time, activity limits, and the review date, and confirms what pain relief is appropriate afterwards.

What to expect

Expect soreness once the anaesthetic wears off, a small wound that scabs and heals over one to three weeks, and sometimes a scar or temporary skin-colour change. Pain is usually manageable with the measures the clinician advises, and the wound should steadily improve day by day.

Limits

Electrocautery has limits: it treats the visible wart, and warts can return. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. It also carries small risks of scarring, infection, and, for larger areas, longer healing, which is why the clinician judges suitability for each person and location.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare is hygiene and observation only: keep the wound clean and dry, leave the scab undisturbed, avoid picking or scratching, and contact a clinician for increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, or slow healing. Attend review even if the wound looks healed.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Laser Removal: Clinician Laser Treatment for Warts
body:
What it is

Laser removal is a clinician treatment in which a focused beam of light energy removes wart tissue in a clinic, usually under local anaesthetic. It is generally reserved for warts that have resisted other treatments, or for warts in locations where precision matters. It requires specialist equipment and trained staff, and it is not a home device treatment.

How it works

The procedure involves anaesthesia, eye protection for everyone in the room, precise application of the laser to the wart, and dressing of the wound. The clinician explains the expected healing time, which is often longer than for freezing, and books a review appointment.

What to expect

Expect soreness after anaesthesia wears off, a wound that heals over two to four weeks, and a scar or skin-colour change in some cases. Healing should improve steadily; a wound that worsens after initial improvement should be reported promptly.

Limits

Laser removal has limits: it treats the visible wart with precision, but it does not remove the virus from surrounding skin. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. It is also the most resource-intensive option, with longer healing and higher cost, so it is reserved for cases where simpler treatments have not worked or are unsuitable.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare is hygiene and observation only: keep the wound clean and dry, follow the clinician's dressing instructions, avoid sun exposure on healing skin as advised, and contact a clinician for increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, or slow healing. Attend review as booked.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: What to Expect During and After a Wart-Removal Visit
body:
What it is

Every wart-removal visit follows a similar pattern, whatever method the clinician chooses: examination and diagnosis first, a discussion of options, the procedure itself, and then wound care and a review date. Knowing this pattern in advance reduces anxiety and helps a person ask useful questions. No method is chosen by the patient alone: the clinician matches the method to the wart, its location, and the person's history.

How it works

During the visit, expect the clinician to examine the area, sometimes with magnification, confirm that the growth is a wart, discuss options and their trade-offs, and agree a method. The procedure itself varies in length from minutes to longer for surgical methods, and pain relief is discussed beforehand.

What to expect

After the visit, expect soreness, a wound or blister that heals over days to weeks, and written wound-care instructions. Most people return to ordinary activities quickly, with limits the clinician states for the wound site. A review appointment is booked to check healing and whether further treatment is needed.

Limits

The limits of any visit are the limits of removal itself: the visible wart is treated, while the virus may persist and new warts can appear. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. A visit also cannot guarantee that one session will be enough; several sessions are common.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare after any method is hygiene and observation only: keep the area clean and dry, follow the clinician's dressing instructions, do not pick at healing skin, and contact a clinician for increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, bleeding that does not stop, or a wound that worsens. Keep the review appointment even if healing looks complete.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Aftercare at Home After Clinician Wart Treatment
body:
What it is

Aftercare at home after clinician wart treatment means only hygiene and observation: keeping the treated area clean and dry, following the dressing instructions the clinician gave, and watching for signs that need clinician advice. It does not mean treating the wart yourself, applying anything new to the area, or trying to finish a removal that the clinician started. The boundary is clear: the clinician treats, the patient keeps the area clean and reports problems.

How it works

Good aftercare starts before leaving the clinic: the clinician's written instructions, the dressing or covering in place, and a clear statement of what to do if the dressing comes off or the area becomes painful. At home, the routine is washing hands, keeping the area clean and dry, changing dressings only as directed, and wearing loose clothing that does not rub the area.

What to expect

Expect gradual improvement: soreness easing day by day, a blister drying or a scab forming, and then new skin appearing. Healing takes days to weeks depending on the method, and some itching as skin heals is common. Improvement that stalls or reverses is a reason to call, not to wait.

Limits

Aftercare has limits: hygiene supports healing but cannot prevent recurrence, and it cannot rescue a wound that is becoming infected. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. If healing is not progressing, the correct step is clinician review, not a stronger home measure.

Aftercare and follow-up

Aftercare steps, in full, are: wash hands before touching the area, keep it clean and dry, follow dressing instructions exactly, avoid picking, scratching, or applying new products without clinician advice, and contact a clinician promptly for increasing pain, spreading redness, pus, fever, bleeding that does not stop, or a wound that opens. Attend review as booked and bring the log.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.

title: Recurrence and Follow-Up Monitoring After Wart Removal
body:
What it is

Recurrence means a wart returning in the same place or appearing nearby after treatment, and it is common after every removal method. Follow-up monitoring means planned review appointments and self-observation between visits, so a returning wart is found early and dealt with by a clinician. Understanding recurrence in advance prevents the disappointment of believing one treatment should have settled the matter permanently.

How it works

Monitoring usually means a review appointment weeks after treatment, then further reviews if the wart persists or returns, plus advice on what to look for between visits. The clinician decides whether to repeat the same method, try a different method, or investigate further if a growth looks unusual or does not behave as expected.

What to expect

Expect review visits to be brief when healing is good, and expect the clinician to ask directly whether anything new has appeared. A returning wart is treated as an expected possibility, not as a failure by the patient, and re-treatment is discussed in the same calm way as the first treatment.

Limits

The limits of monitoring are honesty about its purpose: it finds recurrence early, but it does not stop the virus from persisting. Removal treats the visible wart while the virus may persist, and recurrence happens. Removing a wart does not eliminate the virus from the surrounding skin. Monitoring also depends on attendance: missed reviews mean missed chances to catch a return early.

Aftercare and follow-up

After treatment, keep every review appointment, note any new growth with its date, and contact a clinician promptly if a new growth appears, changes quickly, bleeds, or looks unusual. Keep vaccination and screening up to date alongside wart follow-up, since prevention and monitoring work together.

See a clinician

See a clinician for personal advice, diagnosis, and treatment decisions. This record is educational only. If you notice a new growth, a changing growth, bleeding, pain, or a wound that is not healing, seek clinician advice promptly rather than waiting or attempting any treatment yourself.
